notes.definition: All substances are made of atoms. An element contains only one type of atom, while a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
explanation: All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. An element is a substance made of only one type of atom, and each element is represented by a chemical symbol, for example O for oxygen, Na for sodium and Fe for iron. A symbol starts with a capital letter, and if it has a second letter that letter is lower case (Co is cobalt, but CO is carbon monoxide). There are about 100 different elements, and they are all shown in the periodic table.

You need to know the names and symbols of the first 20 elements: hydrogen H, helium He, lithium Li, beryllium Be, boron B, carbon C, nitrogen N, oxygen O, fluorine F, neon Ne, sodium Na, magnesium Mg, aluminium Al, silicon Si, phosphorus P, sulfur S, chlorine Cl, argon Ar, potassium K and calcium Ca. You also need the Group 1 metals (including rubidium Rb and caesium Cs), the Group 7 halogens (including bromine Br and iodine I) and other elements met in the course, such as iron Fe, copper Cu, zinc Zn, silver Ag and lead Pb.

Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions. A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined (bonded) in fixed proportions, and it is represented by a formula. In water, H₂O, there are always two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom. A compound has different properties from the elements it is made from: sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a toxic green gas, but sodium chloride is table salt. Because the atoms are bonded, a compound can only be separated into its elements by a chemical reaction, not by a physical process such as filtering.

Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances, and they often involve a detectable energy change, such as the mixture getting hot. Reactions can be represented by word equations, for example magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, or by symbol equations using formulae. The substances on the left are the reactants and the substances on the right are the products.

To name compounds from formulae, a compound of a metal and one non-metal usually ends in -ide: NaCl is sodium chloride, MgO is magnesium oxide and FeS is iron sulfide. A compound that also contains oxygen often ends in -ate: CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate, CuSO₄ is copper sulfate and KNO₃ is potassium nitrate. OH in a formula is hydroxide, so NaOH is sodium hydroxide. A small subscript number applies to the atom just before it, and a number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it, so Ca(OH)₂ contains 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H atoms.

In a balanced symbol equation the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides, because atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction, only rearranged. To balance an equation you put numbers in front of formulae (coefficients); you must never change the small numbers inside a formula, because that would change the substance. For example, 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). State symbols show the state of each substance: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous, meaning dissolved in water.
keyFacts: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
There are about 100 different elements, all shown in the periodic table.
An element contains only one type of atom and has its own chemical symbol, such as Na or O.
A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Compounds can only be separated into their elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions always make new substances and often have a detectable energy change.
Compounds of a metal and one non-metal end in -ide; many compounds that also contain oxygen end in -ate.
Balance equations by changing the numbers in front of formulae, never the subscripts.
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
Higher tier: ionic equations show only the ions and substances that change; half equations show electrons gained or lost.

keyTerms.definition: The smallest part of an element that can exist.
A substance made of only one type of atom.
A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Two or more atoms bonded together, for example O₂ or H₂O.
Symbols and numbers showing which elements are in a substance and the ratio of their atoms, for example CO₂.
A change in which one or more new substances are formed, often with a detectable energy change.
A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
A letter in brackets after a formula showing its state: (s), (l), (g) or (aq).
An equation that shows only the ions and substances that take part in a reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An equation showing the electrons gained or lost by one species in a reaction, for example Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

workedExamples.title: Counting atoms in a formula
workedExamples.question: How many atoms of each element are in one formula unit of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, and how many atoms are there in total?
steps: Ca has no subscript, so there is 1 calcium atom.
The bracket (OH) is multiplied by 2, so there are 2 oxygen atoms and 2 hydrogen atoms.
workedExamples.answer: 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H: 5 atoms in total.

workedExamples.title: Balancing a symbol equation
workedExamples.question: Balance the equation for sodium reacting with chlorine: Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s)
steps: Count chlorine: 2 on the left, 1 on the right. Put 2 in front of NaCl: Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
Count sodium: now 2 on the right but only 1 on the left. Put 2 in front of Na.
Check: left 2 Na and 2 Cl; right 2 Na and 2 Cl. Balanced.

workedExamples.title: Writing an ionic equation (Higher)
workedExamples.question: Magnesium reacts with copper sulfate solution: Mg(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Write the ionic equation.
steps: Split the aqueous ionic compounds into ions: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + Cu(s).
SO₄²⁻ appears unchanged on both sides, so it is a spectator ion. Cross it out.
Check that atoms and charges balance: total charge is 2+ on each side.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think any molecule is a compound.
misconceptions.right: In fact a molecule only counts as a compound if it contains two or more different elements. O₂ and H₂ are molecules of elements; H₂O and CO₂ are compounds.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often balance equations by changing the small numbers in formulae, for example writing H₂O₂ instead of 2H₂O.
misconceptions.right: In fact changing a subscript changes the substance (H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide). You may only change the numbers in front of formulae.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a compound keeps the properties of the elements in it.
misconceptions.right: In fact a compound has different properties from its elements. Sodium chloride is safe to eat even though sodium and chlorine are both dangerous.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think symbols like CO and Co mean the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact Co (capital C, lower case o) is the element cobalt, while CO is the compound carbon monoxide, made of carbon and oxygen.

realWorld: Food labels list sodium chloride (salt), a compound of two hazardous elements that is safe and essential in small amounts.
Water treatment works add chlorine compounds rather than pure chlorine gas to kill microorganisms safely.
Fertilisers are labelled by their compounds, such as ammonium nitrate and potassium chloride, so farmers know which elements they supply.
higherTier: Write balanced ionic equations, leaving out spectator ions, for example H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) for neutralisation.
Write balanced half equations showing electrons, for example Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
examTips: When counting atoms, remember that a number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it, and a big number in front of a formula multiplies the whole formula.
After balancing, always check every element on both sides one at a time, including oxygen, which often appears in more than one product.
Write symbols with exactly the right capitals: Cl not CL, Mg not MG. Examiners will not accept the wrong case.
If a question asks for state symbols, include them for every substance; one missing state symbol can lose the mark.
summary: All substances are made of atoms, the smallest part of an element that can exist.
An element has one type of atom; there are about 100 elements in the periodic table.
Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions make new substances and often involve an energy change.
Balanced equations have the same number of each type of atom on both sides.
Higher tier: ionic and half equations show only the particles that change.

questions.question: What is the smallest part of an element that can exist?
markScheme: 1 mark: an atom
questions.explanation: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together, and compounds and mixtures contain more than one substance or element.

questions.question: Which of these substances is a compound?
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₂
questions.explanation: CO₂ contains two different elements (carbon and oxygen) chemically combined. O₂ and N₂ are molecules of elements, and Na is an element.

questions.question: Approximately how many different elements are there?
markScheme: 1 mark: about 100
questions.explanation: There are about 100 different elements, all shown in the periodic table. Only the first 20 are usually learned by name and symbol, which is why some students choose 20.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
markScheme: 1 mark: K
questions.explanation: Potassium is K (from its Latin name kalium). P is phosphorus, Po is polonium and Pt is platinum.

questions.question: How many atoms are there in total in one formula unit of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: 5
questions.explanation: There is 1 Ca, and the 2 outside the bracket doubles both O and H, giving 2 O and 2 H. Total 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Answering 4 comes from doubling only the H.

questions.question: What is the name of the compound with the formula Na₂SO₄?
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium sulfate
questions.explanation: SO₄ is the sulfate group, so Na₂SO₄ is sodium sulfate. Sodium sulfide would be Na₂S, with no oxygen.

questions.question: Which statement about compounds is correct?
options: They can be separated into elements by filtration
They contain elements mixed in any proportions
They have the same properties as the elements in them
They can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions
markScheme: 1 mark: they can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions
questions.explanation: The elements in a compound are chemically bonded in fixed proportions, so a chemical reaction is needed to separate them. Filtration is a physical process, and compounds have different properties from their elements.

questions.question:
Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen:
N₂(g) + __H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
Which number is needed in front of H₂ to balance the equation?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3
questions.explanation: 2NH₃ contains 6 hydrogen atoms. Each H₂ has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 3H₂ is needed. Choosing 6 confuses the number of atoms with the number of molecules.

questions.question: Which half equation shows chloride ions forming chlorine gas?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Two chloride ions each lose one electron to form one Cl₂ molecule, so atoms and charge balance (2− on each side). Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is the reverse process, and adding electrons on the left would not balance the charge.

questions.question: Which is the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions that stay unchanged in solution, so they are left out. The full equation is a balanced symbol equation, not an ionic equation.

questions.question: Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. How many atoms are there in one molecule of glucose?
markScheme: 1 mark: 24
questions.explanation: 6 carbon + 12 hydrogen + 6 oxygen = 24 atoms.

questions.question: How many oxygen atoms are shown by 3CO₂?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6
questions.explanation: Each CO₂ molecule has 2 oxygen atoms, and there are 3 molecules, so 3 × 2 = 6 oxygen atoms.

questions.question: Aluminium sulfate has the formula Al₂(SO₄)₃. How many atoms are there in one formula unit?
markScheme: 1 mark: 17
questions.explanation: 2 Al + 3 S + (4 × 3) O = 2 + 3 + 12 = 17 atoms. A common error is to multiply only the O by 3 and forget the S.

questions.question:
Propane burns in oxygen:
C₃H₈(g) + xO₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)
What is the value of x needed to balance the equation?
markScheme: 1 mark: counts 10 oxygen atoms in the products (6 in 3CO₂ + 4 in 4H₂O)
1 mark: x = 5
questions.explanation: The products contain 3 × 2 = 6 oxygen atoms in CO₂ and 4 × 1 = 4 in H₂O, a total of 10. Each O₂ supplies 2, so 10 ÷ 2 = 5 molecules of O₂.

questions.question: State what is meant by an element.
acceptedAnswers: atoms with the same number of protons
markScheme: 1 mark: a substance made of only one type of atom
questions.explanation: An element contains only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions.

questions.question: Define the term compound.
markScheme: 1 mark: two or more different elements
1 mark: chemically combined (bonded) in fixed proportions
questions.explanation: Both parts are needed: more than one element, and chemical bonding in a fixed ratio. A mixture also has more than one substance but they are not chemically combined.

questions.question: Give two features that show a chemical reaction has taken place.
markScheme: 1 mark: one or more new substances are formed
1 mark: there is a (detectable) energy change, such as a temperature change
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions always form new substances, and they often involve an energy change that can be detected, for example as heating or cooling.

questions.question: Magnesium ribbon burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Write a word equation for this reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
questions.explanation: Reactants go on the left and products on the right, joined by an arrow. Word equations use names, not formulae.

questions.question:
Balance this equation:
Mg(s) + HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
markScheme: 1 mark: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
questions.explanation: MgCl₂ has 2 chlorine atoms and H₂ has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 2HCl is needed on the left. Everything else is already balanced.

questions.question:
Name the compounds with these formulae:
(a) KBr
(b) CaCO₃
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) potassium bromide
1 mark: (b) calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: KBr contains a metal and one non-metal, so it ends in -ide. CO₃ is the carbonate group, so CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.

questions.question: A student tries to balance the equation H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂. Explain why this is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: changing the subscript (small number) in a formula changes the substance / H₂O₂ is a different substance (hydrogen peroxide)
1 mark: balance by putting numbers in front of formulae: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
questions.explanation: The formula of a compound is fixed, because elements combine in fixed proportions. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water. The correct balanced equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.question: Iron is magnetic. When iron and sulfur are heated together they form iron sulfide, which is not attracted to a magnet. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: iron sulfide is a compound / a new substance has formed
1 mark: a compound has different properties from the elements it contains / the iron is chemically combined so no longer behaves as iron
questions.explanation: In the reaction the iron atoms bond with sulfur atoms to make a new substance with its own properties. The iron is no longer present as the element, so the product is not magnetic.

questions.question:
Balance this equation for the extraction of iron:
Fe₂O₃(s) + CO(g) → Fe(l) + CO₂(g)
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 in front of Fe
1 mark: 3 in front of both CO and CO₂: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(l) + 3CO₂(g)
questions.explanation: Balance iron first: 2Fe. Each CO takes one O atom from Fe₂O₃ to make CO₂, and Fe₂O₃ has 3 O atoms, so 3CO and 3CO₂ are needed. Check oxygen: 3 + 3 = 6 on the left, 3 × 2 = 6 on the right.

questions.question:
Zinc reacts with copper sulfate solution:
Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
Write the ionic equation for this reaction and name the spectator ion.
markScheme: 1 mark: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
1 mark: sulfate ion (SO₄²⁻) is the spectator ion
questions.explanation: The sulfate ion is in solution on both sides and does not change, so it is left out. Zinc atoms become zinc ions and copper ions become copper atoms.

questions.question: Write a balanced half equation for a magnesium atom forming a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺.
markScheme: 1 mark: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: A magnesium atom loses two electrons to form a 2+ ion. The charge is 0 on the left and (2+) + (2−) = 0 on the right, so it balances. Writing Mg + 2e⁻ → Mg²⁺ is wrong because adding electrons would make a negative ion.

questions.question:
Methane (CH₄) burns in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.
Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for this reaction, and state what the formula CH₄ tells you about methane.
markScheme: Indicative content: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l); CH₄ shows methane is a compound of carbon and hydrogen; it contains 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms per molecule, in a fixed ratio of 1 : 4.
1 mark: correct word equation
1 mark: correct formulae in the symbol equation
1 mark: correctly balanced with suitable state symbols (H₂O may be (g) or (l))
1 mark: CH₄ is a compound containing 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms (fixed ratio)
questions.explanation: Balance carbon (1 each side), then hydrogen (4 needs 2H₂O), then oxygen (2 in CO₂ + 2 in 2H₂O = 4, so 2O₂).

questions.question:
A student mixes iron filings with powdered sulfur, then heats the mixture strongly. The mixture glows red and a black solid forms.
Compare the substances before and after heating. In your answer, describe and explain the differences in terms of elements, mixtures and compounds, and suggest how the student could show that a chemical reaction has happened.
markScheme: Indicative content: before heating there are two elements, iron and sulfur, each made of one type of atom; they are mixed, not chemically combined; they can be in any proportion; each keeps its own properties (iron is magnetic, sulfur is yellow); they could be separated by a physical method such as using a magnet. The glow shows an energy change (energy is released). After heating a new substance, iron sulfide (FeS), has formed; it is a compound; iron and sulfur atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions (1 : 1); it has different properties (black, not attracted to a magnet); it can only be separated into iron and sulfur by a chemical reaction. Evidence: hold a magnet near the product, compare colour, note the glow (energy change).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear comparison of the mixture and the compound, explaining chemical combination and fixed proportions, with linked evidence for a chemical reaction.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the mixture and the compound with some explanation, and gives at least one piece of evidence for a reaction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example that a new substance forms or that iron is magnetic, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The key contrast is that the elements in a mixture are not bonded and keep their properties, while the compound formed is a new substance with fixed composition and new properties. The magnet test, colour change and energy given out are evidence of a chemical reaction.
